summary: This informational memo discusses the requirements on how IETF output is published. It starts from the point that technical publication is how specifications are disseminated to the community, so the requirements of the publication process should be understood.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo sets out what the IETF expects from the organization that publishes its standards. It covers everything from editing a draft before approval to numbering it, archiving it and announcing it, and it is meant to be used when writing a contract for that job.

questions: what does the ietf technical publisher do
what is the rfc editor responsible for
how long should rfc publication take
subtitle: What the IETF expects from whoever publishes its standards, written down so it can be put in a contract.

tldr.problem: The IETF needs its technical specifications edited, numbered, archived and announced, but the boundaries between what the working groups do and what the publisher does have never been written down as requirements.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists 22 tasks a technical publisher may be responsible for, from editing a document before approval to maintaining the catalogue and the errata, and turns each into a requirement or a goal.
tldr.outcome: The document is meant to be used when writing contracts for a technical publisher, and it is explicitly not a judgement on how the RFC Editor does the job today.

today: RFC 4714 is an Informational memo published in October 2006, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It is a requirements document rather than a specification: it says it is expected to be used when preparing contracts for a technical publisher, and it is not a judgement on how well the RFC Editor fulfils those requirements today.

sections.title: What The Technical Publisher Does
sections.content:
The work of the IETF is to discuss, develop and disseminate the technical specifications that support the Internet's operation, so a published technical specification is one of its main outputs. The IETF technical publisher is responsible for the final steps in producing those publications, and this document sets out requirements on that role and on how it interacts with the IETF.

The term technical specification is used on purpose to mean the technical output of the IETF. The document does not enter the debate about whether that output is expressed as RFCs or otherwise, what an RFC is, or how they should be classified; those questions are out of scope. The intention is to clarify the IETF's consensus on its requirements for its technical publication service, and it is expected to be used when preparing future contracts. It is not a discussion of how well the current technical publisher, the RFC Editor, fulfils those requirements.

Requirements on a publisher can be expressed both as the tasks it is responsible for and as performance targets it should meet; the functions it provides are sometimes called editorial management. The document addresses documents published through the IETF standards process, and the requirements are written in general terms so they can be reused for other publication streams. The list of tasks was derived by looking at what the RFC Editor does now and at what the technical publishers of 3GPP, ATIS, ETSI, IEEE and ITU do.

Four things are deliberately left out: policies on the acceptable input and output formats including figures, policies on acceptable character sets for internationalization, policies on the layout and style of published documents, and policies on the contents of non-technical sections such as acknowledgements and reference classifications. The document acknowledges that those policies are also important to making a published document an IETF product, and that they will evolve with the ongoing IETF discussion, so the publisher should take part in those discussions and be ready to implement changes.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo sets out what the IETF expects from the organization that publishes its standards. It covers everything from editing a draft before approval to numbering it, archiving it and announcing it, and it is meant to be used when writing a contract for that job.

sections.title: The Tasks And Their Requirements
sections.content:
Standards organizations all have technical publication as part of their process, but the boundary between what the technical committees do and what the publisher does varies. The memo lists 22 potential tasks for a publisher and discusses each one in terms of its relevance to the IETF and how it is realized inside the IETF processes, then derives requirements from that discussion.

The tasks fall into groups. Before approval, there is pre-approval review or editing and making a preliminary specification available. Around approval, there is post-approval editorial cleanup, validation of references, validation of formal languages, and insertion of parameter values. Between approval and publication there can be technical corrections, and after publication there are errata. Around the document itself there are the allocation of permanent stable identifiers, conversion into output formats, and translation. Around the queue there is publication status tracking, expedited handling for documents that are needed urgently, and exception handling for documents that must be withdrawn or put on hold. Around the record there are notification of publication, indexing and maintenance of the catalogue, access to published documents, maintenance of a vocabulary document, and publication statistics and status reports. And around the community there are process and document evolution, tutorial and help services, and liaison and communication support.

Each task carries requirements rather than absolute rules. Some tasks produce no requirement at all: the IETF does not need a preliminary version because the approved draft is already available as an internet draft, and IETF specifications are published only in English, so no translation service is required. The memo is careful to say that the publisher should not perform a technical review of a document, only an editorial one.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists 22 tasks a publisher might do, from editing a draft before approval to keeping the archive and publishing statistics. Most become requirements, but a few do not: the IETF needs no preliminary version and no translation.

sections.title: Editing Before And After Approval
sections.content:
Pre-approval review or editing would catch grammar, spelling, formatting and boilerplate problems while the document is still being reviewed, so that the changes can be looked at as part of the technical review. The memo notes that this is not part of the current IETF standards process but was explored in an early copyediting experiment, and that the effectiveness of early editing is still being evaluated. The requirement is that the publisher should be capable of doing it, and should do it before Working Group Last Call, but should not perform a technical review.

Post-approval cleanup is the current practice. Most publishers target light editing, because the dangers of changing agreed text are real. Stylistic editing has in the past produced a substantial number of changes in many documents, and each one then has to be vetted by all the authors and go through further rounds of acceptance and re-vetting, which can add a substantial delay. Changes made to improve readability can also end up affecting consensus wording or technical meaning. The requirements are that the publisher should review the document and try to keep its appearance consistent with earlier ones, that all changes should be tracked and signed off by the appropriate technical representatives including the authors, the document shepherd if there is one, and the Area Director, and that the publisher should exercise restraint in both stylistic changes and readability changes. Where text is the result of careful negotiation, the publisher may be required to publish it verbatim, and in the IETF standards process that can be requested by the IESG.

Three smaller tasks come next. References should be validated, so that all references are currently available and expected to remain so, and publication should be delayed until the required normative references are ready. Formal language sections should be checked with a tool; within the IETF the RFC Editor syntactically validates sections containing MIBs, ABNF, XML and ASN.1. And the publisher should work with IANA to put the assigned parameter values into the documents, without needing technical expertise itself.

Technical flaws can still turn up in the window between approval and publication. The publisher should permit such changes, but only ones approved by the appropriate party, which in the IETF means the authors and the Area Director, and it should alert the Area Director and suspend processing if a requested change looks suspect or unreasonable, such as massive editorial changes. The interaction between authors and publisher has to be policed well enough that untracked and unapproved changes cannot be introduced.
sections.plainLanguage: The biggest argument in this memo is about editing. Fixing a document after approval means every change has to be agreed again by the authors, which slows publication down, and a well-meant rewrite can quietly change what the group agreed. The memo says: be restrained, track everything, and let the Area Director sign off.

sections.title: The Catalogue, Errata And Access
sections.content:
Several tasks are about the record of what has been published. The publisher allocates the permanent stable identifiers, which for the IETF means the RFC numbers, and any additional identifiers as the IESG directs. It maintains the index of all published documents and the permanent archive, stores the meta-information such as status and category and keeps it updated as the status changes, and keeps the archive secure enough that published documents cannot be modified by outside parties. It also keeps the permanent archive of any source documents associated with a published specification. When an authority such as the IESG says a document's status should change, for example to Historical, that must be reflected in the index.

Errata are the corrections identified after publication. The publisher should maintain them and publish the process for reviewing, updating and approving them, which the IETF defines, and the information on relevant errata should be part of the information associated with an RFC. Publication should be announced to the community. The publisher should also provide search tools for finding and retrieving published documents, and those tools should return the associated meta-information, such as the category of the document, whether it is on the standards track, what obsoleted or updated it, and its errata, and they should be integrated with the IETF's own search tools.

Status tracking means being able to say where a document is in the process. Within the IETF the RFC Editor queue gives each document a status such as AUTH48, RFC-EDITOR, IANA or ISR, and items can sit in the queue for a long time without changing. The requirements are that state information be publicly available for each document, that it be integrated with the IETF tools so documents move seamlessly from the standards tracking system into the publication tracking system, and that there be external visibility not only of the fact that a document has been waiting a long time but also of who holds it and why.

Finally the publisher should publish monthly statistics on queue times, documents processed, the types of editorial corrections found and how many the authors rejected, and author-requested changes, plus a status report at each IETF meeting, and it should participate in discussions about how the process and the documents evolve, keep guidance for authors, run tutorials and a help desk at IETF meetings, and take part in IESG meetings through a liaison.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of this is the archive. The publisher owns the catalogue, keeps the record of what each document is and what replaced it, holds the errata against it, and publishes statistics so outsiders can see how the process is doing.

sections.title: Performance Goals
sections.content:
Publishers are measured on what they do and on how well they do it. The expectations in this section are treated as goals rather than requirements, for two reasons. Achieving a given level of performance is not entirely under the publisher's control, because publication is a process and the goals are goals of the process rather than of the publisher alone. And the actual performance objectives will be set contractually, so the values in the document are the ones the IETF community feels are desirable and reasonable for work progress, without regard to financial or other factors.

Publication timeframes measure the time from a document entering the publisher's queue until it is published. Long publication times cause internal difficulties, such as authors migrating to other activities and the accumulation of tempting post-approval fixes, and external difficulties, such as other standards organizations being unable to reference IETF publications for lack of an RFC number. The community's consensus is that an average publication time of under a month is desirable, that there will sometimes be delays outside the publisher's control, and that the time required for a pre-approval review should be under 10 days.

Publication throughput is the number of documents published in a given period, sometimes also given in pages produced, with the counts separated by document category. The goal is that although minor variations are expected, there should be no long-term growth trend in the length of the publication queue.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo also sets targets: a document should take less than a month to publish on average, a pre-approval review under ten days, and the queue should not get steadily longer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There is a tussle between the improvements in readability that editing aims for and the specific language that has often been negotiated carefully for the security content of IETF documents. As with other text, extreme caution is needed in modifying anything in the security considerations section, and the memo says this issue is assumed to have been dealt with by the rules on post-approval editing.

The publication processes should prevent the introduction of unapproved changes, which is the subject of the section on post-approval technical corrections. And because the publisher maintains the index of publications, enough security should be in place to stop published documents being changed by external parties.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules matter here. Never let an unapproved change slip into a published document, and make sure the archive cannot be edited from outside.

items.title: Before approval
items.text: Pre-approval review or editing, and making a preliminary version available.

items.title: Editing and validation
items.text: Post-approval editorial cleanup, checking references, checking formal languages, and inserting parameter values.

items.title: Technical corrections
items.text: Fixing technical flaws found between approval and publication, and publishing errata afterwards.

items.title: Identifiers and formats
items.text: Allocating permanent identifiers, converting the document into output formats, and translating it.

items.title: Tracking and priority
items.text: Tracking the status of each document, expediting some of them, and handling withdrawals and holds.

items.title: The catalogue
items.text: Maintaining the index and archive of published documents, and giving access to them.

items.title: Support
items.text: Maintaining a vocabulary document, publishing statistics, helping the process evolve, running tutorials and a help desk, and liaising.
